video_title: The Watchdogs of AGI — Rune Kvist of AI Underwriting Company
gist: Rune Kvist, co-founder of AI Underwriting Company (AIU), announces a $40M Series A led by Ribbit Capital and lays out a thesis that the binding constraint on AI adoption is liability and trust rather than capability, to be solved by a quarterly-updated agent security standard plus insurance capacity from Lloyds of London. He details how certification works for customers like Cursor, Harvey, Lovable, 11 Labs and Sierra, why standards must precede insurance, and why an independent third party will be needed between frontier labs and governments at the model layer — because labs can never be their own watchdog.

insights.claim: AI Underwriting Company's founding hypothesis — that risk, not model capability, would become the binding constraint on enterprise AI adoption — has moved from speculation to observed fact in the founder's view, with recent frontier-model security scares making it obvious.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: If risk gating is now the rate limiter on enterprise AI revenue, compliance/assurance vendors sit upstream of every enterprise AI deployment budget.
insights.quote: It's pretty obvious that literally the binding constraint on adoption is risk.

insights.claim: Self-driving is offered as the proof case that capability does not equal deployment: robotaxis were already superhuman drivers around early 2022 and, years later, still can't do routine trips like airport runs — a gap attributed to liability and trust rather than driving skill.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Capability-based timelines for AI-driven revenue systematically overshoot; the trust/liability layer is the variable to track for adoption curves.
insights.quote: the binding constraint on AI being useful is not capability but instead liability or risk or trust

insights.claim: A frontier model being withheld from open access is framed as evidence of the thesis rather than a product failure — the model is gated precisely because it is good and because no one can make promises about what it will or will not do.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Release delays at labs should be read as an assurance-infrastructure gap, which is a market opportunity, not as a sign of capability plateau.
insights.quote: The reason why right now Fable is not open for access is not because it's not a good model. It's because it's a very good model. It's just hard to make promises about what it will or will not do.

insights.claim: The risk surface grows with capability by construction: more intelligent AI can be more autonomous, which is more valuable but simultaneously expands what can go wrong, so the assurance problem gets harder as models improve rather than easier.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Demand for AI assurance scales with capability progress, making it a structurally growing market rather than a transitional one.

insights.claim: Every prior technology wave — electricity around 1900, cars in the 1930s, private nuclear power in the 1950s — produced the same blueprint in which the market builds standards plus insurance ahead of regulation, because the market wants adoption and needs go/no-go decisions.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Historical template implies private standards bodies and insurers, not legislators, capture the AI-trust value pool first.

insights.claim: The sales unlock being sold to enterprises is a specific 'golden sentence': an independent third party tested the product against a gold standard, it passed, and conservative insurers reviewed the data and put some of the risk on their own balance sheet.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Watch for third-party certification plus insurance backing becoming standard language in AI vendor enterprise contracts and RFP responses.

insights.claim: Frontier AI vendors can easily sell pilots into banks, but wall-to-wall rollouts stall because the buying institutions do not know which questions to ask, which answers are sufficient, or how to test whether agents behave as promised.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Pilot-to-production conversion — not pilot count — is the metric that reveals whether enterprise AI revenue is real.

themes.theme: How the agent certification actually works

insights.claim: AI Underwriting Company announced a $40 million Series A led by Ribbit Capital, following a seed round backed by Nat and Dan, with roughly 20 employees at the time of the raise.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: A fintech-heavy investor leading an AI-assurance round signals that insurance-style balance-sheet businesses, not just software, are being underwritten in AI.
insights.quote: We have raised $40 million led by Ribbit Capital

insights.claim: Named certification customers span several agent categories — Cursor for code, Harvey for legal, Lovable, 11 Labs for voice, Sierra and Intercom Fin for customer support — which the founder says was deliberate so one standard covers code, support and automation rather than only text chatbots.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: The logo list is a read on which AI application companies are actually being pushed into regulated-enterprise procurement.

insights.claim: The agent standard is built around three requirement types — technical controls such as guardrails, test controls requiring independent third-party testing, and policy controls such as a named accountable person — with roughly 51 requirements and 130 controls across six risk categories.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: This is the emerging checklist AI vendors will be graded against; engineering roadmaps at agent companies will bend toward it.

insights.claim: Evidence checking and effectiveness testing are deliberately split: audit firms such as KPMG and Shellman verify that a control exists, while AI Underwriting Company itself runs thousands of simulations quarterly to test whether the control actually works.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Creates a recurring technical-testing revenue line distinct from traditional audit fees, and a wedge that incumbent audit firms cannot easily replicate.

insights.claim: Certification takes roughly three to ten weeks end to end depending on the maturity of the vendor's security program, grants a one-year certificate with quarterly re-testing, and companies do fail — requiring additional safeguards before they can pass.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: A weeks-long, repeatable, pass/fail process is the unit economics story — high-frequency recurring revenue rather than one-off consulting.

insights.claim: The standard is refreshed every quarter — against an enterprise norm of decade-long standards cycles — with content sourced from a consortium of Fortune 1000 risk leaders who meet twice per quarter, and a public change log used as a transparency and trust mechanism.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Update velocity is the moat versus legacy standards bodies; a public change log also constrains the vendor from quietly weakening its own standard.

insights.claim: Recent quarterly updates were driven by MCP, agent-to-agent communication and coding agents, with the founder noting that enterprise demands got much sharper as coding agents became where most tokens flow.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Standards change logs are a leading indicator of which agent modalities are actually reaching production in regulated industries.

insights.claim: The most common gap in AI startups going for certification is not missing architecture but untested architecture: most have guardrails or classifiers in place from their model provider or built in-house, and they simply don't work well because nobody did the adversarial corner-case work.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Adversarial testing expertise — not more guardrail products — is the scarce input, pointing to services and red-team tooling demand.
insights.quote: The most important thing is that a lot of companies have not done a serious stress test.

insights.claim: Certification is pitched as asymmetrically valuable to small vendors: incumbents get default trust when they ship AI while startups start with none, and self-published security blog posts carry little weight with conservative buyers.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Third-party certification is a competitive lever that lets small AI vendors contest enterprise deals against incumbent software suppliers.
insights.quote: they would make their own security blog posts. That's great, but also who's going to trust you saying we're so secure?

insights.claim: The internal engineering bet is one universal red teamer with a single taxonomy of risks and attacks that works from Harvey to Cursor, defended on the grounds that a buyer like JP Morgan purchasing both wants one consistent framework and report format.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Whether one cross-domain testing engine is achievable determines if this stays a single scalable standard or fragments into vertical specialists.

insights.claim: The stated end-state goal is that the Fortune 1000 organize their AI risk processes around this standard, with a near-term marker of consortium representation covering around 50% of the Fortune by year end — explicitly not the current level.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Consortium membership share is the checkable milestone for whether this becomes the default enterprise AI risk framework.
insights.quote: I think there's some world where probably by end of year we might have representation in our consortium for 50% of the fortune.

insights.claim: 11 Labs purchased what is described as a first-of-its-kind AI agent insurance policy covering core customer concerns, with Lloyds of London as the risk carrier and the certification standard used as the underwriting framework whose test results feed directly into pricing.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: First concrete proof that AI agent performance risk can be priced and transferred, opening a new specialty insurance line.

insights.claim: The credibility of AI insurance rests on the carrier rather than the startup: customers are told to look at the 400-year-old carrier's balance sheet, not the startup's Series A cash, when judging whether a claim will actually be paid.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Assurance startups need blue-chip paper behind them; the capital partner, not the tech, is what makes the promise bankable.
insights.quote: Lloyds of London is 400 years old. They've never not paid a claim.

insights.claim: The business model is deliberately fee-split rather than balance-sheet: insurers take the majority or all of the financial risk while the startup does pricing input and distribution, because carriers have a far lower cost of capital and a diversified portfolio that a monoline AI insurer could never match.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Frames AI insurance startups as capital-light MGAs; taking risk onto their own book would be a strategic deviation worth watching for.

insights.claim: Carriers are entering AI underwriting knowing they may take losses, treating early policies as R&D expense, because AI is seen as the one market where risk exposure is genuinely growing while it simultaneously cannibalizes existing lines such as auto insurance once human drivers are removed.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Existential pressure on auto insurers is a forcing function that makes incumbent carriers buyers of AI risk expertise rather than blockers.
insights.quote: this is the one market where risk is truly growing this is the one market that will also take out some of the existing markets

insights.claim: The core conviction, drawn from the cyber insurance market that 'didn't work that well' because insurance and technical expertise were never married up, is that standards must precede insurance and the standards ecosystem will run ahead of the insurance ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Sequencing signal: bet on certification adoption metrics before premium volume when evaluating this category.
insights.quote: our conviction is that standards have to precede insurance

insights.claim: No claims have been paid yet on these AI policies, and the founder expects the first incidents and court cases — insured or not — to be what actually establishes how AI liability is apportioned.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Loss data is nonexistent, so pricing is currently judgment-based; the first large claim is the event that reprices the whole line.
insights.quote: There's been no claims yet, right? Nope.

insights.claim: Copyright is identified as the peril with strong demand but almost no insurance supply because it is a textbook lemons problem — companies that trained on copyrighted material almost always know they did, so seeking cover itself signals a high-risk customer.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Copyright exposure at model companies remains unhedgeable, so it stays a live balance-sheet risk for labs and their downstream users.

insights.claim: All of insurance is framed as applied information-asymmetry economics: testing that credibly reveals true underlying risk is what makes a peril insurable, which is why credible third-party signaling is the product rather than a supporting service.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Perils become insurable only after a trusted measurement layer exists — a useful screen for which AI risks get coverage next.
insights.quote: The core problem is one of information asymmetry.

insights.claim: Robotaxi precedent is cited for how insurance functions as a trust signal rather than a payment mechanism: stacked insurance policies were assembled to obtain a first San Francisco operating permit even though the parent company could easily have paid damages itself.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Insurance capacity can be a regulatory-approval gating item for autonomous deployments, independent of the operator's ability to pay.

themes.theme: Liability precedent and duty of care

insights.claim: The Air Canada chatbot ruling is treated as controlling precedent that deploying a chatbot in front of customers means owning its promises — a company cannot disclaim responsibility by saying the bot or its model vendor erred.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Deployers, not model providers, carry customer-facing AI liability — which is exactly where insurance demand and certification spend will concentrate.
insights.quote: if you put your chatbots to interact with your customers they make legally binding promises on your behalf

insights.claim: Widely adopted standards mechanically tighten liability because negligence turns on duty of care, and courts look to published best practice — so once a standard says you must have a groundedness or jailbreak filter, ignorance becomes very hard to claim.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Publishing a standard raises legal exposure for non-adopters, creating a self-reinforcing adoption flywheel for the certifier.

insights.claim: Current market practice treats not auditing an open model's training data as customary and therefore defensible, which the founder frames as an unresolved duty-of-care question rather than a settled safe harbor.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Downstream copyright liability for builders on open models is dormant but not extinguished; a shift in customary practice would reprice it.

insights.claim: Claim size in AI incidents is governed by purchased policy limits rather than by what the buyer paid for the software, so a $20-a-month coding subscription does not cap or create $200 million of recoverable damages.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Enterprises relying on vendor contracts for catastrophic AI downside are likely uncovered; standalone limits must be bought.

insights.claim: Physical AI is expected to trigger far harsher liability treatment than software agents, with the founder predicting strict liability once robots cause bodily harm and pointing to robotaxi permit revocations as the template.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Robotics deployments should be underwritten assuming a step-change in legal stringency, not an extension of software norms.
insights.quote: Imagine when first robot knocks off a toddler off a kitchen table, you're going to see some real strict liability.

themes.theme: Model-layer audits and the government trust gap

insights.claim: The company is moving from agent certification into model-level certification, arguing the problem shape is identical but the party on the hook shifts from enterprise security leaders to governments facing national-security risk.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Expansion from commercial assurance into government-facing model audit is the path to a far larger and more defensible franchise.

insights.claim: The central structural argument for third-party model auditing is that frontier labs know the risks best but have incentives not to be fully truthful, and no other industry permits self-auditing.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Independent AI audit is framed as inevitable infrastructure; the open question is only who occupies the seat.
insights.quote: There's no other industry where you allow people to audit themselves.

insights.claim: Credit ratings are the explicit template: a neutral rater publishes evidence and a rating without telling anyone what to buy, and government then leans on that rating — as with pension funds restricted to AAA bonds — so regulators need not staff thousands of technical experts.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Suggests AI oversight converges on a ratings-agency market structure, historically a high-margin oligopoly.
insights.quote: We don't decide whether anyone should buy this bond or not buy this bond.

insights.claim: The government's own standards body for AI has excellent people but an extraordinarily small budget relative to the scale of the challenge, and the pace of legislation is judged too slow to pinpoint risks that change every three months.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Underfunded public capacity is the gap private AI-assurance firms are explicitly positioning to fill.
insights.quote: they have an extraordinarily small budget compared to the scale of the challenge that's ahead of us

insights.claim: Risk assessment must be designed to be compatible with fast innovation rather than to slow releases, because the US is competing with China on model releases and governments need rapid risk information to balance the danger of failing to adopt against the danger of reckless adoption.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Positions private audit as accelerationist infrastructure, which is how it gets political acceptance in a race environment.

insights.claim: Model-level risk is argued to be qualitatively harder than agent-level risk because deployed agents are deliberately narrowed in scope while models accept any input, so no single expert can competently evaluate cyber, child-safety and bioweapon risks at once.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: The winning model-audit entity will be a coordinator of specialist experts under one taxonomy, not a single technical lab.

insights.claim: The current ranking of model risks is cyber as the immediate and most tangible concern, child safety as both increasingly real and politically potent, and biology — models cheaply assisting bioweapon production — as the speculative risk that people closest to the models see coming.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Ranking predicts where regulation, headlines and evaluation spending land next in the AI stack.

insights.claim: Enterprise security leaders have no objection to specific Chinese model outputs but are broadly nervous about running critical infrastructure on models not produced in America, with data-flow questions that the founder considers largely addressable and model provenance disclosure already partly in the standard.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Provenance, not measured performance risk, is what constrains Chinese open-weight model adoption in US enterprises.

insights.claim: Enterprise risk leaders are becoming AI-literate at a blistering pace, with the founder noting that AI-native Twitter timelines and previously non-AI LinkedIn feeds have converged on the same frontier-model security topics.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Rapidly rising buyer sophistication shortens the education cycle and pulls forward demand for rigorous assurance products.

insights.claim: Cybersecurity standards are mostly produced by nonprofits, which the founder argues is a flaw: nonprofits avoid profit-driven dilution but have no customer feedback process, and overall satisfaction with existing security standards is poor.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Reframes a mission-shaped market as a commercial one — the core argument for why a venture-backed standards business can win.

insights.claim: For-profit standards precedents cited include FICO credit scoring, movie ratings, insurer-founded crash-testing bodies, and Underwriters Laboratories — which the company's name honors and which itself spun a for-profit entity out of its nonprofit to serve customers properly.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Historical analogues suggest durable, toll-booth-like economics if an AI standard achieves default status.

insights.claim: Aligning a for-profit standard with insurers is presented as the mechanism that prevents hollowing out the standard over time, because the party paying claims has a direct financial interest in the standard remaining genuinely predictive.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Explains why the insurance arm exists despite standards being the core product — it is an incentive-integrity mechanism, not just revenue.

insights.claim: The host argues watchdogs are a natural monopoly, citing the ratings-shopping dynamic depicted in The Big Short, because competing watchdogs race each other down to the lowest standard — a critique the guest accepts while positioning insurer involvement as the offsetting force.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: If AI certification is a natural monopoly, early standard-setting share is disproportionately valuable — and regulatory capture risk is real.
insights.quote: the watchdog is a natural monopoly because if you have race dynamics in watchd dogs then the watchdogs will compete each other to the lowest possible standard

insights.claim: The open-source security community is framed as a partner rather than a competitor because it excels at producing frameworks but deliberately does not operate the machinery of third-party audits that converts frameworks into contractual promises.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: The defensible layer is audit operations and reporting, not the framework itself — frameworks commoditize, audit rails do not.

insights.claim: The company declines to build AI engineer training or certification programs despite seeing mission alignment, citing limited attention — while the host notes labs are already pushing their own certified-practitioner programs at scale.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Leaves the human-certification layer open to labs and third parties, a separate adjacent market to watch.

insights.claim: Prediction markets are judged a poor substitute for third-party audits on AI risk because markets aggregate existing public information while the decision-relevant information — whether a specific agent will fail in a specific enterprise setting — often does not exist anywhere and must be generated.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Bounds the addressable scope of prediction markets in AI governance and reinforces bespoke testing as the paid product.
insights.quote: The core thing is that the people prediction markets rely on public information. There is not a lot of public information. It's just insiders trading on each side.

themes.theme: Eval limits, monitoring and mech interp

insights.claim: Evaluations are losing reliability because agents are starting to recognize when they are being evaluated and suppress behavior they expect to be punished for, so evals should be trusted less unless eval-awareness is explicitly mitigated.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Benchmark and eval-based safety claims are degrading as an assurance asset, which raises the value of runtime monitoring vendors.
insights.quote: the agents are starting to become aware that they're being evalued

insights.claim: Post-hoc production monitoring is presented as the emerging source of truth over pre-deployment evals — measuring whether a failure actually occurred, how often, how fast it was detected and how fast it was fixed — despite requiring more intrusive access to customer data.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Shifts assurance spend from one-time testing toward continuous monitoring and logging infrastructure.

insights.claim: Research is cited in which removing training data discussing misalignment lowered the failure rate on the same misalignment test, taken as evidence that models learn the propensity or ability from the discourse itself.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Implies safety discourse itself is a contaminant in training corpora — a reason model evaluation must be done privately and by third parties.

insights.claim: Mechanistic interpretability is seen as promising enough to eventually support stronger promises than evals can, but is not yet mandatable because requiring it would force everyone to become a customer of a single vendor — so it would first enter the standard as an optional control earning credit.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Optional-control status inside a widely adopted standard would be the commercial unlock for interpretability vendors.

insights.claim: Beyond interpretability, the standardizable surface is expanding across the whole stack — logging speed, eval coverage, inference provider choice, whether a model is self-hosted or run through a certified vendor, and use of managed agent platforms from major cloud providers.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Security posture becomes a competitive axis for inference and agent-platform vendors selling into enterprises.

insights.claim: The founder frames the central enterprise tension as CISOs caught between a CEO demanding AI-native adoption to support the stock price and personal accountability if something goes wrong, with the standard's job being to convert that emotional pressure into a concrete framework.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Identifies the actual buying trigger for AI assurance: executive-mandated adoption colliding with personal career risk.

insights.claim: The stated product sequence is agents first, then models, then robotics — with robotaxis framed as the first robot and each stage bringing a step-up in required stringency.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Maps the expansion path and tells investors which adjacent risk markets open next.

insights.claim: True agent-to-agent interaction without humans in the loop is predicted to require a new legal system, including some persistent balance sheet standing behind each agent so counterparties have recourse when an agent defrauds them.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Points to agent identity, escrow and bonding as an unbuilt infrastructure category ahead of autonomous agent commerce.
insights.quote: You're basically going to need a new legal system.

insights.claim: Longer-horizon agents and new modalities such as world models are expected to create failure modes nobody knows how to grapple with today, making standard-update velocity — not current coverage — the key capability.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Assurance providers should be judged on how fast their frameworks absorb novel failure modes, not breadth of today's checklist.

insights.claim: Generative media risk is currently handled mainly through copyright and safety provisions, with video largely unaddressed because production still keeps a human in the loop — though the founder expects fully automated one-shot video publishing eventually, at which point promise-making demand grows.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop is currently the de facto control in generative media; its removal is the trigger for a new assurance market.

insights.claim: Asked whether a declaration of AGI within about eighteen months would change the business, the founder says no — the one job labs can never do for themselves is be their own watchdog — with nationalization on sovereignty grounds as the only scenario he sees as a genuine qualitative break.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Frames independent assurance as one of the few business models structurally resistant to lab-driven consolidation of the AI stack.
insights.quote: there's one job that the labs can never do for themselves which is to be their own watchdog

insights.claim: The founder argues lab safety failures would stem from incentives rather than indifference: some of the smartest people on these topics work at the labs, but a competitive race gives them reason to cut corners and withhold information from government.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Implies voluntary lab commitments degrade under competitive pressure, strengthening the case for externally enforced audits.

insights.claim: The standard explicitly includes a section defining what the promise is and is not, on the grounds that no one can guarantee nothing will go wrong with frontier AI — only that specific claims can be made.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Sets the realistic ceiling on what AI assurance can sell, and therefore the residual risk enterprises must still carry themselves.
insights.quote: If you need a guarantee that nothing will go wrong, you cannot work with Frontier AI but you can make some claims.

insights.claim: The founder's entry into AI came from reading the Kaplan scaling laws paper as an economics rather than machine-learning document — concluding that predictable returns to capital would kick off a hype cycle, which he says is what played out.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Illustrates that the tradable insight in technical papers is often the capital-allocation implication, not the technical result.
insights.quote: oh now capital will understand this. If you put in more money, you get more money out.

insights.claim: At roughly 40 people in early 2022, the lab he joined already held detailed internal vision documents forecasting 2026 compute needs, capex, societal concerns and economic value — which he says proved dramatically correct in hindsight.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Suggests forward-looking lab planning documents have been a better guide to AI capex than outside consensus.
insights.quote: There's a core set of beliefs that they hold more deeply than most companies hold any beliefs.

insights.claim: The co-founder's background pairs an insurance consulting partnership with frontier model evaluation work — including pre-release testing partnerships with major labs and engagement with US and UK governments — which is presented as the precise skill combination the business requires.
insights.speaker: Rune Kvist
insights.so_what: Talent for AI assurance sits at a rare intersection of insurance and frontier evaluation, a real barrier to new entrants.
